title: Two ways to ask
prompt:
You want an AI to find the hypertensive patients in your data. Which
prompt will get you better code?

**Prompt A**

> Write R code to find the hypertensive patients.

**Prompt B**

> I have a data frame called `visits`. `sbp` and `dbp` are blood pressures
> in mmHg, stored as numbers; `sbp` has one missing value. Write R code
> that keeps patients whose systolic is 140 or more, or whose diastolic is
> 90 or more. I expect three patients.
hint:
The AI can't see your data, and it can't read your mind. What would it
have to guess from Prompt A?

options.text: B — without it, the AI has to guess the column names, the threshold, and how to handle the missing value
options.feedback:
Right. The AI can't see your data, so everything it isn't told, it
guesses: what the data frame and columns are called, which threshold
counts as hypertensive, whether *either* number being high is enough,
and what to do with a missing reading. Prompt B answers each of those.

It isn't that longer is better. Every sentence in B answers a question
the AI would otherwise answer for you, silently. And the last sentence
gives you a way to check the result.

options.text: A — a short prompt leaves the AI free to choose the best approach
options.feedback:
The approach isn't the problem. A leaves the AI to decide things only
you can decide — which threshold, what counts as hypertensive — and to
guess things it can't see, like your column names.

options.text: B — longer prompts always get better code
options.feedback:
B is better, but not because it's longer. A long prompt full of
background wouldn't help. B works because each sentence answers a
question the AI would otherwise guess: names, threshold, missing
values, and what result to expect.

options.text: No real difference — the AI will work out what's meant
options.feedback:
It will work out *something*, and the code will run. But "hypertensive"
has more than one definition, and the AI will pick one without telling
you. The next exercise shows what that does to the result.

title: Decisions nobody asked for
prompt:
Given Prompt A — *"Write R code to find the hypertensive patients"* — an
AI wrote:

```r
library(dplyr)
hypertensive <- visits |> filter(sbp >= 130 | dbp >= 80)
```

`|` means *or*. Which of the AI's decisions are clinical ones, that should
have been yours? Choose all that apply.
hint:
Some of these change which patients end up in the result. Others only
change how the code looks.
setup:
visits <- data.frame(
  id      = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
  age     = c(58, 71, 65, 49, 80, 66),
  sbp     = c(128, 152, NA, 141, 135, 162),
  dbp     = c(82, 94, 88, 91, 76, 99),
  on_meds = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.text: Using 130/80 as the threshold
options.feedback:
A clinical decision. The 2017 American guidelines start hypertension at
130/80; European guidelines use 140/90. Either can be right for your
study — but the AI chose without saying so.

And it matters: on this data, 130/80 flags **all six** patients. At
140/90, it's three. One decision nobody made doubled the count, and
nothing in the code or the output says a decision was made at all.

options.text: Counting a patient if *either* number is high, rather than both
options.feedback:
A clinical decision too, hidden in a single character: `|` means *or*.
With `&`, *and*, far fewer patients would qualify.

options.text: Using dplyr's `filter()` rather than square brackets
options.feedback:
A style choice. Either way of writing it can give the same patients —
this changes how the code looks, not who's in the result.

options.text: Calling the result `hypertensive`
options.feedback: Just a name. It doesn't change which patients are in the result.

title: Write the prompt
prompt:
You want the average systolic pressure for patients on medication, and for
patients not on medication. Here's what `str(visits)` shows:

```
'data.frame':  6 obs. of  5 variables:
 $ id     : num  1 2 3 4 5 6
 $ age    : num  58 71 65 49 80 66
 $ sbp    : num  128 152 NA 141 135 162
 $ dbp    : num  82 94 88 91 76 99
 $ on_meds: logi  FALSE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE
```

Write the prompt you'd give an AI. Three things make a prompt work:

- **Have** — what the data looks like: names, what the values are, any
  quirks
- **Want** — exactly what you need back, including any decisions only you
  can make
- **Check** — how you'll know the answer is right
hint:
Which columns does the task need? What kind of values are in each? Is
anything missing that could affect an average — and what should happen to
it?

response.exemplar:
I have a data frame called visits. The column sbp holds systolic blood
pressure in mmHg, as numbers, with one missing value. on_meds is TRUE or
FALSE. Write R code that gives the mean sbp for patients with on_meds
TRUE, and the mean for patients with on_meds FALSE. Leave the missing
value out, and also tell me how many values each mean is based on, so I
can check it against the data.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt name every column the task needs? (It needs a systolic pressure column, plus a column saying whether each patient is on medication.)
rubric.on_fail:
**Have:** name the columns the task needs. The AI can't see your data,
so it will guess what they're called — and a wrong guess either fails
or, worse, quietly uses the wrong column.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt say what kind of values those columns hold — for example, numbers in mmHg, or TRUE/FALSE?
rubric.on_fail:
**Have:** say what's *in* the columns — numbers in mmHg, TRUE or FALSE.
The AI writes different code for numbers than for text, and it can't
tell which you have.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt say what should happen to the missing systolic value?
rubric.on_fail:
**Want:** one systolic reading is missing. Say what should happen to
it — left out, or something else. If you don't, the AI decides, and a
missing value can turn an entire average into `NA` or vanish without
a word.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt include a way to check the result — such as asking how many values each average is based on, or stating an expected result?
rubric.on_fail:
**Check:** give yourself a way to know it worked. Asking how many
values each average is based on is a good one — you can count those
yourself in the data.

title: The best follow-up
prompt:
The AI hands you code. Which follow-up is most likely to show you what
could be wrong with it?
hint:
Which question does the AI have the least incentive to answer with
"yes, it's fine"?

options.text: "List every decision this code makes that I didn't specify."
options.feedback:
Right. This asks for exactly what you can't easily see: the gaps the
AI filled — a threshold, how missing values are handled, which rows
are kept. Once they're listed, you can check each against what you
meant.

options.text: "Is this code correct?"
options.feedback:
This invites reassurance. AI models lean towards agreeing with you,
and "correct" can only mean "matches what you asked" — so anything you
didn't specify, it can't flag as wrong. Asking for the decisions it
made gets you further.

options.text: "Make this code better."
options.feedback:
You'll get *different* code, but "better" isn't something you can check.
The new version may make new decisions you didn't ask for.

options.text: "Explain this code line by line."
options.feedback:
Useful for learning what the code does. But it explains what's there,
not what's *missing* — the decisions you never made won't stand out
unless you ask for them directly.

title: Something you've never seen
prompt:
You asked for an age-group column — under 65, and 65 and over. The AI
wrote this, using a function you haven't met:

```r
visits$age_group <- cut(visits$age, breaks = c(0, 65, Inf),
                        labels = c("under 65", "65 and over"))
```

It looks right. Use the routine for anything unfamiliar: **name it** (what
might `cut()` do?), **look it up** if you like, then **try it on something
small where you know the answer**. Run this in the box above it:

```r
cut(c(64, 65, 66), breaks = c(0, 65, Inf),
    labels = c("under 65", "65 and over"))
```

Which group does a 65-year-old land in?
hint: Run it and read the middle value.
setup:
visits <- data.frame(
  id      = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
  age     = c(58, 71, 65, 49, 80, 66),
  sbp     = c(128, 152, NA, 141, 135, 162),
  dbp     = c(82, 94, 88, 91, 76, 99),
  on_meds = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.text: "under 65"
options.feedback:
Right — and almost nobody would guess it. `cut()` makes groups that
include their *upper* boundary by default, so 65 falls into the group
that ends at 65. Patient 3, aged exactly 65, would be labelled "under
65". Adding `right = FALSE` moves the boundary the other way.

Nothing in the code, the name, or a quick read would tell you that.
Trying it on a value that sits exactly on the boundary does. Boundaries
are where code most often disagrees quietly with a clinical
definition, so they're always worth one test.

options.text: "65 and over"
options.feedback:
That's what the labels say, and what you'd expect. Run the line above
it and look at the middle value: `cut()` puts 65 in "under 65".

options.text: `NA` — it falls between the groups
options.feedback:
It does land in a group. Run the line and look at the middle value — 
it's not the group you'd expect.

title: A whole script at once
prompt:
An AI hands you a 40-line script in five steps: read the data, clean it,
add a column, filter it, and summarise it. What's the best way to use it?
hint: If the final number is wrong, how would you find out which step went wrong?

options.text: Run it one step at a time, checking each result before the next
options.feedback:
Right. If you only check the end, a wrong answer could have come from
any of five places — and a *plausible* wrong answer wouldn't send you
looking at all. Checking each step as you go catches a problem where
it starts.

Notice what this means: how much code you *ask for* and how often you
*check* are separate choices. You can take a whole script at once and
still run it in pieces.

options.text: Run all of it, then check the final number
options.feedback:
If the number looks wrong, you won't know which of the five steps
caused it. And if it looks *right* but isn't, you won't look at all.
Checking each step catches a problem where it starts.

options.text: Ask the AI to give it to you one line at a time instead
options.feedback:
That works — and in unfamiliar territory it can be worth it. But it's
slow, and you don't need it to check as you go: you can take the whole
script and still *run* it one step at a time.

options.text: Read it carefully, then run it all
options.feedback:
Reading helps, but many problems don't show on the page — a column
stored as text, a missing value, a boundary. Running each step and
looking at what it produced shows what reading can't.

title: When the whole thing is fine
prompt:
Checking every step isn't always worth the time. In which of these is it
reasonable to take a whole script and check only the end result?
hint: When would a wrong result be obvious at a glance?

options.text: Remaking a kind of plot you've made many times before
options.feedback:
Right. You know what it should look like, so a mistake shows at a
glance, and little rides on it. Checking step by step pays off when
you *can't* tell a wrong answer from a right one by looking — new data,
new tools, numbers that matter.

options.text: The first analysis of a dataset you haven't looked at yet
options.feedback:
This is where step-by-step matters most. You don't yet know the data's
quirks — text in a number column, a value in the wrong unit — and each
step is a chance for one to slip through.

options.text: Numbers that will go into a paper or a report
options.feedback:
The higher the stakes, the more it's worth checking each step. A
plausible wrong number in a paper is exactly what you're trying to
avoid.

options.text: Code that uses a package you've never used
options.feedback:
New tools are where surprises live — like `cut()` putting 65 in the
wrong group. Step by step, with small tests, is the safer way here.

title: Rewrite a weak prompt
prompt:
Someone asked an AI:

> Add a column for high blood pressure.

Rewrite it so the AI has nothing important left to guess. You want each
patient labelled "high" or "not high", using 140/90, where either number
being high is enough. Here's the data again:

```
'data.frame':  6 obs. of  5 variables:
 $ id     : num  1 2 3 4 5 6
 $ age    : num  58 71 65 49 80 66
 $ sbp    : num  128 152 NA 141 135 162
 $ dbp    : num  82 94 88 91 76 99
 $ on_meds: logi  FALSE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE
```

Use **Have**, **Want** and **Check**.
hint:
Which decisions did the original leave to the AI? There are at least three
— and one patient's systolic is missing.

response.exemplar:
I have a data frame called visits, with systolic (sbp) and diastolic (dbp)
blood pressure in mmHg, stored as numbers. sbp has one missing value. Add
a column called bp_status that says "high" if sbp is 140 or more OR dbp
is 90 or more, and "not high" otherwise. If sbp is missing, decide using
dbp alone. Then tell me how many patients are "high" — I expect three —
and list any assumptions you made.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt name the blood pressure columns the code should use?
rubric.on_fail:
**Have:** name the columns — the AI can't see them. Without names, it
guesses.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt give the threshold as specific numbers — 140 systolic, 90 diastolic?
rubric.on_fail:
**Want:** give the numbers. "High blood pressure" has more than one
definition, and the AI will choose one for you — 130/80 flagged every
patient in this data.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt make clear that either number being high is enough (systolic OR diastolic)?
rubric.on_fail:
**Want:** say whether *either* number being high is enough, or both
must be. That one word changes who's included.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt say what should happen when the systolic value is missing?
rubric.on_fail:
**Want:** one patient's systolic is missing. Say what should happen —
otherwise the AI decides, and that patient may quietly get the wrong
label, or none.

rubric.criterion: Does the prompt include a way to check the result, such as an expected count of patients or a request to list assumptions?
rubric.on_fail:
**Check:** add a way to know it worked — the number of "high" patients
you expect, or a request to list the assumptions it made.
